I's a big struggle. As a movie that is surreal, this movie could be a great movie (even though it's rated 13), but mixed with the use of the director's relatives playing the roles, due to the use of the word "family" ... which in this case, is not just a use of that word, it's giving it a new meaning, a whole new meaning! However, if you're into surreal movies (there are some that are great, actually, like the Japanese ones, for example), you might be able to overlook the family (pun relatives) and enjoy this movie. There are great ideas here, after all! Many people hate this ambiguous movie, but while watching this (with a group of friends) almost all of us were crying tears, from laughing so hard,, including the director of course! However, everyone has their own opinion, as you can see by the high ratings of this movie, but I would highly recommend the movie if you like any of the work that Alejandro Jodorowsky has done and/or are a fan of his!

I've read the book 'Scarlett' and was expecting a good movie the first time I saw it. I'm afraid to say that I was disappointed. The movie did not follow the book and made many changes that I did not like. One of the changes that I did not like the way that Lord Fenton was portrayed. It made no sense to make him out to be a bad man. The way that things ended between Lord Fenton and Scarlett was a lot different and their whole relationship was too intimate. There was also a lot less confrontation between Scarlett and Rhett in the movie than was originally written in the book. The movie sent the two in two completely opposite ways and they did not seem to cross paths often enough to make it seem like there still could be love between the two. I had read the book 'Scarlett' and was expecting a good movie the first time I saw it. I'm sorry to say that I was disappointed. The movie was not bad, but there were many things that I did not like. One of the things that I did not like was the way that Rhett was portrayed. They made an effort to make him out to be a good guy. The way that things developed between Ashley Fenton and Rhett was not believable, and it seemed to happen too quickly. There was also a lot of confrontation between Scarlett and Rhett in the book that was not shown in the movie. Also, by the time the two finally parted ways, they did not seem to cross paths often enough to make it believable that there still could be love between the two. A fine movie, but I think that it certainly could've been better than it was, had it more true to Alexandra Mitchell's book..

Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a failed Swedish book editor who decides to take a non-stop train to Berlin. Unfortunately for everyone around him, he's a walking disaster, causing mayhem everywhere he goes. The train also holds a man and his mistress scheming to murder the man's wife (who's also on the train), a soldier on his way home, two gay elderly gentlemen, an angry train conductor, two nuns, a bunch of refugees, and even more people. Meant as a mix of noir-ish thriller (which it does quite well - at least to begin with), and comedy, the film fails with both. It doesn't sit right as the film changes tone with every new scene. And as the train races towards its final destination, the film turns more and more bizarre, ending on a truly surreal note. The good bits are wasted in a myriad of pointless plots and characters. Skenbart is packed with famous Swedish actors, no matter how small the part is. It feels like the filmmakers rang everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part in the film. Too bad that the performances are just as bad as the script (act your lines - don't read them!). The comedy is more or less slapstick, with the same jokes repeated over and over. The pace is incredibly slow at times (quite often, actually) with on scene in particular dragging on for about ten minutes for no good reason. The screenwriter also seems to think that swearing is a good way to replace decent dialogue. The film looks great though, in moody B&W, but it's wasted on such inept film-making in every other department. [1/10]

Set in 1945, Skenbart is a German comic book man who decides to take a non-stop train to Berlin. As a comic book character, he's a walking disaster, causing mayhem wherever he goes. The train also carries a bunch of other people, including the comic book man's wife (who's also on the train), a woman on her way home, two middle old gentlemen, an angry young woman, two young girls, a bunch of refugees, and even more people. Meant as a mix of drama, science fiction (which it does - well - none of to begin with), and comedy, the film is a mess. It doesn't sit right as the film changes tone with each new character. And as the train heads towards its final destination, the film becomes more and more bizarre, ending on a rather surreal note. The good bits are wasted in a sea of confusing plots and weak characters. The film is packed with famous German actors, no matter how small their part is. It's like the filmmakers rang everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part in the film. Too bad that the performances are written as well and the actors (actresses) are struggling to read their own lines. The comedy is more or less non-existent, with the same jokes repeated over and over. The pacing is incredibly slow at times (especially on the train) with on scene in particular dragging on for over ten minutes for no good reason. The director seems to think that casting is more important than making a decent film. The visuals is good though, in colour and B&W, but it's wasted by the ineptitude of almost every other aspect. [1/5]

Had the League been me pitching this script, the BBC would probably have turned around and said "no - we can't take the money - this is dreadful". I've always enjoyed the League's work, but this is their poorest effort to date. It's slow, not particularly funny, there are few laugh out loud moments. They do exist, but they are few and far between. Also, the format is a bit unoriginal. The feeling is that the writers were writing for money, and it shows, not for being a fan. Even the original Xmas special had better production values - the FX here are pretty poor and it is clearly obvious that they didn't film in the original location (in Vasey - they filmed this on the cheap in Manchester). The musical score is weak and the editing is poor. Also, the performances of the cast were way off from their TV equivalents. The cast, including the lead (Simon Fton), just didn't feel like it. It's a shame, because I was hoping for a really good special. This really is the League's equivalent of the Xmas special - but without the quality of the TV series.

I, like most other people, saw this movie after hearing of it from Patton Oswalt. Oddly enough, it was easier to find than I thought it would be. Though, it shouldn't come as a surprise that I found it used. The plot is summed upped masterfully within the title. It's a bed that eats. Nothing more, nothing less. There is an effort to throw in a story line but not a very good one. A demon's blood ended up on a bed and, as a result, it becomes possessed. It devours anything that happens upon it by absorbing and then dissolving it in what appears to be orange Fanta. There is an artist who fell victim to the bed, but was sick and ends up behind a painting in the room it inhabits. The narrative is told entirely through him. This movie fails horribly at everything, even at being bad. Still, it's not without its own brand of charm.

I, like many of you, saw this movie after hearing of it from friends and family. Oddly enough, it was easier to watch than I thought it would be. I know I shouldn't be saying this, but I found it entertaining. The movie is summed upped pretty well by the title. It's a bed that talks. Nothing more, nothing less. There's no need to throw in a story line that isn't a good one. A demon's blood ends up on a bed and, as a result, it becomes animated and then talks to anyone who sleeps on it. The bed then drinks a can of what appears to be orange Fanta. It follows an artist who fell asleep on the bed, but gets sick and ends up behind a painting in a room full of paintings. The narrative is told entirely through the bed's perspective, which fails to explain everything. It really is bad. Still, it's not without its own charm.

In this follow up to Edge of Civilization, we see the last years of Quentin Crisp's life in New York. John Hurt is not Crisp (come on who doesn't know the man) but rather a character he inhabits to the point of disappearing. For me Hurt is Crisp and I've always found it so hard to take the man himself seriously that I couldn't believe he was himself. Its masterful work. His performance is nuanced and subtle, as is Robin Norton, who as his his friend and confidant. Unfortunately, beyond the performances the film has little to recommend it. To be honest the film serves the man, rather than the other way around. Visually, the film looks and feels like New York and its a beautiful film, but dramatically it kind of sucks. We see him talking to people in bars,trying to come to terms with the world he lives in (he ended up regretting some of his words about AIDS) and dealing with the infirmities that old aged thrust upon him. Quentin the man is very interesting, but his life as portrayed here is not. I am disappointed by the film. I am fascinated by the man and his life and his work. I just wish he was better served by the film about his life.

Trite and unoriginal. It's like someone watched Immortal Beloved and Amadeus and decided to mix them together and, in the process, steal other formulaic plot parts from other movies to make another one. As with most historical movies nowadays, there are some inaccuracies as history is manipulated to better suit the story, which is understandable for the most part. For example, during the remaining days of Beethoven's life, it was necessary for other people to write down what they needed to say in order for him to understand them. That, of course, would have been a nuisance to have to show on screen. The script, although filled with some quotable lines, doesn't quite capture the feel of that time period and, coupled with some bad acting, seems rather contemporary. Diane Kruger is nice enough to look at but she still has lots to improve on her craft. Ed Harris doesn't work for me as Beethoven and I mostly blame Gary Oldman for that. Overall, not a very good interpretation of the musical maestro's life. Better just find yourself a copy of Immortal Beloved. http://iwascalledclementine.multiply.com/reviews

This movie is a mess. It's like someone watched Immortal Beloved and Amadeus and decided to combine them, but then felt the need to steal other scenes and plot points from those movies to make this one. As with most biography movies nowadays, there are some instances where history is altered to better suit the story, which is particularly problem in this case. For example, during the remaining years of Mozart's life, it was common for other people to write the pieces they wanted Mozart hear, order for him to play them. That, I imagine, would have been a nuisance to have to show on screen. The script, although filled with some quotable lines, doesn't quite capture the feel of the time period and, combined with some bad acting, seems very forced. Diane Kruger is nice enough to look at, but she has lots to improve on her acting. Ed Harris doesn't work for me either, and I mostly blame Gary Oldman for that. Overall, not a very good interpretation of the great maestro's life. Instead, find yourself a copy of Immortal Beloved. http://iwascalledclementine.multiply/

This movie would have been alright, indeed probably excellent, if the directors would have left the interviews and the concert footage separate. "Into the Void" is a great song, and I hate how it is cut off at the best part to go to an mumbling interview with Ozzy Osbourne. That should have been at the end of the film, or located in a special feature. The best part of concert DVDs is to put them on and let the music play, but "Black Sabbath: The Last Supper" is hard to put and and simply let play because the music is continually interrupted. Nevertheless, there are a few strengths to this film; the concert footage, when it does play, it excellent. Black Sabbath returns to the stage after a long hiatus without Osbourne and this film captures that well: Sabbath basically rocks the fans. The fans, of course, have a sweet advantage in the film because they are seeing the band live, of course, but also they do not have to put up with the incessant interviews that the DVD viewers are burdened with. Shame on Jeb Brien and Monica Hardiman (the directors) for doing this to the film! Also, shame on Wyatt Smith for editing the film in such a way.

"Black Sabbath: The Last Supper" is hard to watch and I simply cannot play because the music is continually interrupted. However, there is a positive side to this film. The concert footage, when it is shown, is excellent. Ozzy returns to the stage after a long hiatus without incident, and the film captures how well Black Sabbath basically owns the fans. The fans, of course, have a sweet advantage in this film because they are there at the concert, of course, but also they do not have to put up with the incessant interviews that the DVD viewers are burdened with. Shame on Sean O Brien and Monica O'Brien (the producers) for adding interviews to the film. Also, shame on Wyatt Brown for editing the film in such a way

This is absolutely the worst movie I've ever seen. It's hard to explain, but it's just a a bad movie. I bet you've never seen a movie that isn't good or bad; it just is. (That's the worst part-not good or bad, just is.) Let me say that I have seen plenty of movies without a main character and I like them all. That's what makes this such a mystery. The supporting leads are terrible acting (even the dialog is bad). The only character that is fairly good is the one played by John Goodman. He does a pretty good job with what little material he has, and actually has one funny line (I won't spoil the only funny line in the movie, in case you decide to watch it and turn into a pancake). The big mysteries are the supporting leads. I won't say their names, because no characters are even developed. This script is so bad that they don't even use any of the characters fictional names. They don't use their faces. They don't even seem to be reading their lines. It's as though they are all reading out loud to themselves from a script that the local grocery store sent to them. I've seen better acting like this in my English class in college, and it wasn't funny. So this movie isn't funny. It isn't interesting. It isn't exciting. It just happens to have the worst acting and dialog you can imagine in it. I just couldn't even sit through the whole thing. It was so boring I couldn't even work up the irritation needed to turn it off. I can't imagine how this is even getting a rating of 4 here.

One day Bob and Marion Boxletter see a man at their hotel. Marion thinks it is her long lost brother Brian, but when they see him he appears to be a complete stranger with exactly the same face. They manage to get his fingerprints and send them to the police, where the identity is confirmed that it is in fact Brian. So Marion and Bob leave for New York, tracing his steps. They get a hold of Brian, but still he has no idea who they are talking to. But the only thing they want to know is that Brian has their faces, maybe from a year or two ago... and even when they see him he doesn't recognize them either. The plot suggests that they will find themselves one day thinking that they are someone else as well. Experiments made out on people seem to be the explanation here, yet the logic of why they would bother putting Bob and Marion in the same building as each other is beyond my comprehension. Gregory Peck and Audrey Hepburn are great, but I have no idea what is up with the other actors, they look bored and lost. 3 out of 10, a little strange yes but interesting..

The acting is good, but for the most part the movie as a whole is just cheesy. Shirley Jones' character makes so many references to her being a nun that we started counting and after a while we were giggling every time she said it. Add to that the "love theme" played incessantly throughout the film and we couldn't wait for it to be over so we could enjoy the evening more.

Okay, I love Italian horror films. The cheesier they are, the better. However, this is not cheesy Italian. This is day-old pasta sauce with a horror spoon. There is an hour on every scene. There is no suspense, jump scares, with only a few drops of blood scattered around to remind you that you are in fact watching a horror film. The "special effects" consist of the walls seeming to move when the ghost (as if there was ever a ghost) is around, and the girl's bed sheets turning upside down. Oooh, can you feel the chills? Aside from the ridiculous quality of the dialogue (which actually makes the film more entertaining than it should be), this is below even the lowest standards of horror. The only reason I gave it one star is because the dialogue is so hilarious. And when we finally discover that she really DOES live in the attic (in a house that is daytime one moment and night the next)...well, I won't spoil it for anyone who really wants to know, but let's just say that the ending is... "novel."

I thought Hollywood had promised to NEVER make another "Noah" movie again, but sadly that doesn't seem to be the case. In addition to the bland and uninspired acting of the whole cast (except for Noah'syle, who undoubtedly gave the best of his career in this film), the story line has been completely convoluted. I also don't see how Noah was able to stay focused on the ark for the 40 days, since he was so teary-eyed and dazed all the time. The script writer obviously had very little knowledge of the book of Genesis, or just didn't care that his audience would enjoy a story that mocked it.

I understand, and others have carried this idea off much more successfully, but I think it's a mistake to move between the two extremes here (period piece vs. action film). Just because this is a "modern" retelling, doesn't mean that it has to look like a period piece, or have anything to do with action or violence. If the filmmakers had embraced the subtlety of the original play, Macbeth would be a far more interesting film. As it is, read the Shakespeare. Read it out loud. Ask your Oxford dictionary the questions. Skip the film. Oh, but I'm not done. This is enough for a day-long review. IMDb needs me.

This frothy romantic comedy is based on the kind of story I loved as a teenager, but now find rather distasteful. In the case of May-September attachments, doubtless what is on the mind of the elder party is either lust, or an inability to face the reality of aging, or both. And the younger is most likely looking for the kind parent that she (or he) lacked as a child. These underlying agendas seem more pathetic than romantic to me now; there is also something rather predatory about them. Dick Powell looked a bit embarrassed--as well he should--at playing the elder lover in this silly story. He was, at fifty, attempting the role of a thirty-eight-year-old man romancing a teen-ager. But young Debbie Reynolds was a knockout--pretty and saucy and full of vinegar--as a misbehaving seventeen-year-old presented as a kind of "gift" to the morally upright and honest screenwriter, as a subject for him to study. Her spirited performance wrung from me a better rating than this film would otherwise deserve. Anne Francis was cast as Powell's beautiful, but brittle fiancée, and handled her small role deftly. Some of the dialogue was quite amusing, too, so it's not a total washout. 5/10

Steered text
This frothy romantic comedy is based on the kind of story I enjoyed as a teenager, but now find rather distasteful. In the case of May-December attachments, doubtless what is driving the actions of the elder partner is either loneliness, or an inability to face the reality of aging, or both. And the younger is most likely looking for the parental attention that she (or he) lacked as a child. These underlying agendas seem more sinister than romantic to me now; there is also something rather predatory about them. William Powell looked a bit ridiculous--as perhaps he should have--as the elder partner in this silly comedy. He was not at all convincing in the role of a thirty-eight-year-old in love with a teenaged girl. However, Debbie Reynolds was a revelation--smart, saucy and full of energy--as a beautiful, rebellious seventeen-year-old cast as a kind of "pet" for the morally upright and honest Powell, and as a subject for him to study. Her spirited performance wrung out a much higher rating than this film would otherwise deserve. Anne Francis was cast as Reynolds's beautiful, but naive, best friend, and handled her small role with dignity. Some of the dialogue was quite amusing, too, so it's not a total washout. 5/10

I have no idea how accurate the portrayal of Flynn appears in this film but even as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The script is all over the place and leaves you wondering how he got from one scene to the next - you are just not given the minimum information needed to keep some continuity and understand his present situation, and it is difficult to understand Flynn's and other characters' motives behind some of their behaviour. Add to that a series of silly and implausible situations and you have film that comes across as one of your dreams that seems to make sense while you are asleep, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is just strange, disjointed and totally unrealistic. There are many long, boring musical sections of the film that to me are either bad direction or a bad director trying and failing to be artistic. None of the characters are even likable and the Flynn character comes across as a self serving liar, thug, thief, robber, murderer, bear fist fighter, gigolo and impostor who will do anything and step on anyone to further his own dreams, and somehow, despite all that, great opportunities just seem to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining nor satisfying in any way and by all accounts not even historically accurate, so why even watch it? To rub salt into the wound, the DVD had one of the worst transfers I have ever seen, it wasn't even in wide-screen or Dolby 5.1, it had terrible telecine wobble and many, many artifacts from what looked like a film reel that had been gathering dust and scratches somewhere.

I have no idea what the production team of this film were thinking, but even as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The plot is all over the place and leaves you wondering how they got from one point to the next - you are not even given the minimum information needed to follow the continuity or understand the current situation. This makes it difficult to understand the story, the characters' motives and some of their behaviour. Add to that a lot of unrealistic and implausible events and you have something that comes across as one of your dreams that seems to make sense while you are asleep, but when you wake wake up and try to remember it, it is jumbled, disjointed and totally nonsensical. There are also long, drawn-out sections of the film that to me are either poor direction or a bad director trying and failing to be artistic. None of the characters are even likable and the main character comes across as a self-serving liar, thug, thief, liar, murderer, killer, fighter, conman and impostor who will do anything and step on anyone to further his own dreams and ambitions, yet despite all that, great opportunities just seem to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining or satisfying in any way and by all accounts not even historically accurate, so don't watch it. To rub salt into the wound, the DVD was one of the worst transfers I have ever seen, it wasn't even in wide-screen or Dolby 5.1 and it had terrible grain, wobble and many, many scratches from what looks like a film print that has been gathering dust for years.

Although I always admired the acting abilities of Joanne Lumley and Timothy Dalton, this is a really terrible film. His mother writes an autobiography which is hailed (despite her protests) as a sort of feminist manifesto. The book is well-written, engaging, and long. Its prose is simply beautiful. This movie, on the other hand, is about Robin Williams once again telling us to seize the day.

Who the heck is responsible for this terrible, terrible movie adaptation of a great book? This is just awful. Bad acting, bad script. The story is not even close to its original form, and what were they thinking casting Robin Williams, for Gosh's sake! This is just a disaster. Don't watch it. Seriously, don't. Not even rent it. It's just a terrible, terrible adaptation, and everything is disjointed and scrambled - the characters which are important in order to understand the sequence of events are seriously marginalized, and the potentially interesting location of the story has been changed (example: Vienna - New York) to make it more accessible. For those who haven't read the book - it's basically a story about a young writer growing up, exploring his sexuality and so on. His book is an autobiography and is hailed (deservedly) as a sort of feminist classic. The book is well-written, engaging, and long. Its prose is just beautiful. This movie, on the other hand, is like watching your grandfather again telling you about his first day.

If you find it hard to sleep one night then play Beyond Rangoon on your VCR and you'll be snoring in no time. Pointless and pretty silly film that is just basically a compilation of clips from horror, science fiction and suspense films. There are unnecessary shots to an audience watching the clips and Donald Pleasance and Nancy Allen are among audience members who turn to the camera and explain why we love horror films. Not a bad idea but all the explanations are obvious ("movie horror helps us deal with real horror", "you are at the mercy of the filmmaker in a theatre") and pretty trite. Also the clips are shown very quickly and the changes are kind of jarring. And, shown out of context, these bits aren't very scary at all. And it's REAL short--I saw it in a theatre back in 1984 and was outraged that I paid $5.00 for an 84 minute movie! Still, it is reasonably well-edited and Allen and Pleasance seem to be enjoying themselves. For people who have an interest in knowing more about terror this might be fun and interesting. But if you're a horror fan (like me) you'll probably be bored silly. Good idea, bad execution (no pun intended). I give it a 3.

Pointless and pretty short film that basically just shows a bunch of clips from movies, TV, and radio shows. There are also shots of an audience watching the films. Donald Pleasance and Nancy Allen are the audience members who turn to the camera and explain why they love horror films. Not a bad idea, but the reasons are obvious ("you are forced to deal with real fear", "you are at the mercy of the filmmaker and the theatre") and pretty trite. Also the clips are not very good and the transitions is kind of jarring. Some clips seem out of place, and others aren't really horror at all. It's also REAL short (I saw it in the theater back in the 80s and was shocked that it was over $100 for an 84 minute film). Still, it is reasonably well-edited and Allen and Pleasance seem to know their roles. For people who have an interest in learning more about horror this might be interesting and informative, but for those who are horror fans (like me) it will probably just look silly. Good idea, bad execution (no pun intended). I give it a C.

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is generally maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as mentally bridging some of the jump cuts in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

Creakiness is what this film has, but it's a good print of the novel. Raymond Bland's laid-back Sherlock Holmes is almost comically dressed in early scenes in his usual attire, but he trades it for a laborer's garb when he visits the home of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What's more, if Holmes was a man, he would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If, in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off with her fiance, he would have done the logical thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After a an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is nowhere to be seen for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of drummers at the scene of Violet Stoner's murder is merely coincidental, and what could have been a good murder tool - a poisonous snake - is ruined by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the snake's movements notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though the sinister performance he gives to Sir Nigel Bruce is not my cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is quite menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1939's "The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated cuts between scenes and an unsteady camera, it's a wonder the story line isn't more confusing than it is. But the dialogue is generally good, even if it stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I, that would be my only complaint with the film, is that bridging some of the gaps in the story line proved to be a real pain in the aspic

Put simply, this mini-series was terrible. Let me count the ways. 1. Absurd plotting. 2. Over-acting. 3. Scattershot approach to characters. 4. Annoying narration. 5. Inability to create viewer interest. This film can't even pass the "Soap Opera for Dummies" test. I'm sorry I have not read this award-winning novel, so I am judging it only as a film, but it really stinks. Imagine going to a party where they show you dozens of appetizers. You look at the wide variety and want to taste them, but suddenly they are withdrawn, and you wonder where they went. That's like this film, with way too many characters introduced and never drawn out. There are enough stories and characters in this film to create a 20 episode series, yet we are given less than four hours to digest it all. There are more facial expressions and reaction shots of Ed Harris than you'll find on 10,000 monkeys. The pace is extraordinarily slow. Dennis Farina and Helen Hunt are so far over-the-top that their characters are not believable. Joanne Woodward's character is one-dimensional. The persistent river metaphor becomes trite. And, probably the most absurd part of the film--the cat. This evil and vengeful cat who follows the hero around to scratch him and his seat covers--well, come on now---it's not even good Stephen King! Probably the most interesting character in the film, and one who is not drawn well, is John Voss, the disturbed boy whose final act of desperation accounts for the only plot device that works in this film. Just about everyone in this film is unbelievable. To sum up, there's little here to inspire. The drama is poor melodrama. It's just a terrible effort.

Oh my, this mini-series is terrible. Let me count the ways. 1. Terrible plotting. 2. Over-acting. 3. Disjointed approach to storytelling. 4. Overwhelming background music. 5. Inability to hold my interest. This film is not even drama. "Soap opera" is a better description. I'm sorry I did not read the award-winning novel, so I am judging it only on the film, but it really is terrible. Imagine going to a restaurant where they show you all the dishes. You marvel at the wide variety and want to taste them all. Then they are withdrawn, and you wonder where they went. It's like this film, with way too many characters, and too drawn out. There are enough stories and characters in this film to create a 20-hour epic, but we are given less than four hours to digest it all. For every 10 facial expressions and reaction shots of Ed Harris, you'll be on 100 shots of the monkeys. The pace is painfully slow. Dennis Farina and Helen Hunt are by far over-the-top and their characters are not believable. Joanne Woodward's character is one-dimensional. The persistent river music becomes a distraction. The worst of the film's plot is the character of the cat. This evil and vengeful cat who teaches our hero how to wear diapers and car seat covers--oh, come on now---it's not even good Lion King! Probably the most interesting character in the film, and the one who is drawn well, is John Voss, the detective, whose innerness and desperation make for a interesting plot line that, in the end, is overwhelmed by the rest of the film's plot. To sum up, there's nothing here to inspire. The writing is poor melodrama. The acting is just terrible.

My guess is that the producers of this low-budget space/horror film wanted a serious movie but the director had his heart set on a parody. So...this is what we get. Set in an abandoned spaceship 1000 years in the future and peopled with characters and props right out of the 90's. The set is some industrial complex, maybe an oil tanker, whatever. They use is AS IS so the controls consist racks of old TV equipment. One location is obviously the employees lunchroom and sports an old TV and VCR as well as a water cooler with plastic demijohn. Tiny Lister and Coolio get the best lines, arguing throughout the story. The dialog is packed with terms that are pretty dated even now ("A-OK, Daddy-O") but then maybe the 30th century is very retro? When the captain declares the ships cargo is a load of coffins from "The Transylvania Station" you know this is all a put-on. Its a bit of Alien, part JasonX, shameless rip-off of all the best sci-fi and horror titles. At one point Casper VanDien even tells his pilot to "make it so" with a straight face. This film would have been better if they had just let everyone run with the satire but they keep attempting to make the story serious....maybe the backers were on the set that day. Anyway, not a bad boredom killer if you aren't too picky. FX are as good as the sets are bad.

My guess is that the producers of this low-budget space/horror film wanted a serious movie but the director had his heart set on a parody. So...this is what we get. Set in an abandoned space station 1000 years in the future and it's filled with characters and props straight out of the 80s. The set is some industrial complex, like an oil tanker or whatever. They station is old, so the controls consist racks of old computer equipment. One location is obviously a doctor's office and another has a TV and VCR as well as a waterbed and a lot of furniture. Tiny Lister and Coolio get the best lines, arguing over the story. The dialog is packed with terms that are pretty outdated even today ("VHS", "VHS") but then maybe that's why they're trying to be retro. When the captain declares the "There is a load of coffins in the back of the station" you know it's all a put-on. With a bit of Aliens and JasonX, shameless rip-offs of all the classic sci-fi and horror titles. At one point Dr. VanDien even tells his monster to remove his mask so we can see his face. This movie would have been better if they had just let it run with the parody but they kept trying to make it more serious. Maybe the backers were afraid the director's vision. It's not a bad boredom killer if you're not too picky. FX are as good as the actors are.

Though a fan of shock and gore, I found this movie disappointing to say the very least. The effects and puppet work were impressive, yes, and the humor was well-timed, but... something was missing. See, the first act of the film is spent establishing nuances of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his aggression is delivered within minutes of the first title cards. As for the narration and many of the flashbacks: needless. The pacing during the second act was tedious. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger eating, then vomiting, then eating some more, then flailing his arms and saying something snappy or rude. All the while, the schlock is punctuated with brief scenes of Jack discussing his rage problems with a therapist. (Definitely the entertaining scenes in the film -- excellent dialog worth plenty of laughs.) Then, without warning, Jack decides to kill a few monsters. And then it's over. All in all, as a throwback to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has loads of potential but is purposeless and plods on without conflict or adequate resolution. Hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks VII: Jack Goes to Hell or Jack vs. Ash go into production.

As a fan of shock value and horror, I found this movie disappointing to say the very least. The effects and special effects were good, yes, and the humor was good at times, but the substance was missing. The first half of the movie is spent on exposition of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his character is revealed within minutes of the opening title cards. As for the narration and most of the flashbacks: needless and uninteresting. The second act was worse. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger eating, then vomiting, then eating some more, then flailing around trying to do something, don't ask. All the while, the schlock is punctuated by brief scenes of Jack discussing his rage problems with a therapist. (Definitely the best part of the movie -- but not worth all of it.) Then, without warning, Jack decides to try and to Freddy. And then it's over. All in all, as a comedic homage to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has loads of potential but meanders it and plods on without conflict or adequate tension. Hopefully, hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks dies: I want to see Jack Brooks vs. Freddy go. :)

I rented a "Straight To Video Independent Horror Film" Walking out with my much better rentals, I went home, popped Dark Harvest in the DVD player and it began. I figured I would watch the trailer after the film was done (BAD IDEA) but went ahead and watched it anyway. NOW to the review.*POSSIBLE SPOILERS* First off, the acting by the "kids" sucks, and the scene when the 2 (main characters) are talking, the lighting sucks, and the buildings even look fake! Now they go to this house, where Sean Connel's (I think he's the main character, I don't care) relatives lived there. All of a sudden one by one, they all start getting killed by...(gasp) A KILLER SCARECROW!!!! AHHH!!!!! And then at the end...they shoot the scarecrow with a gun (that is red for god's sake and looks like it was purchased at a local family dollar) and it pauses for a while and then.....(gasp) BLOWS UP!!!!!! Save yourself some time, I'm telling you this movie sucks. if you need to pass an hour and a half, look at the wall, because looking at the wall is A+ fun compared to this disaster. It is quite funny though. Overall Grade: F If there was anything lower **F-** Than I would give it that.

I was in Blockbuster and I saw a film called "Dark Harvest". The cover art looked great, the title was a and catchy, and the tagline (You reap what you sow) made the movie look pretty good. Maybe I was dumb that day, because I did something I should have never done. I rented a "Straight To Video" Horror Film. Walking out with my much better rentals, I went home, put Dark Harvest in the DVD player and started watching. I thought I would watch the trailer before the film itself. (BAD IDEA) I went ahead and watched it anyway. Now to the movie.*WARNING:JOR SPOILERS* First off, the acting of the "kids" sucks, and the scene when the kids and the "mother" are talking, the lighting sucks, making the scene even more fake. Now we go to this house, where the Connel's (I think that's the main character, I don't remember) relatives are staying. All of a sudden one by one, they start to get killed by...(gasp) A SCARECROW! OHHH!!!! AHHH!!!!! The acting is terrible, the makeup is low budget, and the scene where the scarecrow is talking is so fake it's ridiculous. It makes a sound and everything! And then at the end...they stab the scarecrow with a knife (that's red for god's sake and looks like it was purchased at a dollar family store) and it turns into a humancrow and.....(gasp) dies's the end of the movie. Save yourself the time, and the money, this movie sucks. if you need to spend an hour and a half, look at the wall, I would give the wall an A+ grade compared to this movie. The trailer is funny though. Overall Grade: F If there was a lower "F" grade Than I would give it that

This movie is based on the series Street Fighter Alpha (or Zero)! It is placed in an other setting than Streetfighter the animated movie! This movie is all about Ryu who is accompanied by Ken and Chun Li. I recognized Rose,Zanghief and Birdie! There weren't any other characters used from the video game (that i could discover)! The fighting scenes were OK but nothing really spectacular! And there were not many of them! To me this is odd! Isn't Streetfighter about fighting! Streetfighter the animated movie (1994) is far superior to this movie. It tries to be more than it really is! The use of the "Hada Power" and other supernatural elemnents have nothing to do with skills the characters have in the video game! And in this case that is a bad thing! The story is so boring that you don't really care what is happening! The action is toned down considerably! Why? And what happened to the other characters from the video game! Surely they are more interesting than the villain in this story! The main attraction of the video game are the characters with their own special skills! In this movie it is all about Ryu! That is why this anime fails!
